product.title: Portuguese 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 in European Portuguese: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Portuguese builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. This is the Portuguese of Portugal — not Brazil — from its swallowed vowels and hissing *s* to its everyday habits like *chamo-me*, *estou a falar* and *o meu pai*. Each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip English speakers up: noun gender, the two verbs for "to be", verb endings that let you drop "I" and "you", the contractions *no, na, do, da*, and pronouns that hook on behind the verb.

blocks.text: Here's something worth knowing before you open the first unit: **you already know a lot of Portuguese.** Not just because both languages borrowed heavily from Latin, but because English took some words straight from Portuguese sailors and traders.

*Veranda* is *varanda*. *Marmalade* is *marmelada*. *Flamingo*, *albino*, *cobra*, *molasses* (*melaço*) and *pagoda* all came through Portuguese. And Latin did the rest: *a família*, *o hospital*, *o hotel*, *o museu*, *a música*, *o problema*, *a nação* (nation), *a estação* (station), *a televisão*, *a cidade* (city), *possível*, *importante*, *diferente*.

Spot the pattern in those last words: English *-tion* is Portuguese *-ção*, English *-ty* is often *-dade*, English *-ble* is *-vel*. Learning Portuguese, for you, is partly a matter of **recognizing** — not memorizing from zero.

The second piece of news is about sentence structure, and it takes some getting used to. Portuguese drops its subject pronouns. *Sou inglês* means "I'm English" — with no word for "I" in it, because the verb form already says who's talking. English can never lose its *I* or *you*; Portuguese loses them all the time. Once your ear trusts the verb endings, this becomes a real shortcut.

So where are the difficulties? In three places, and all three are put up front so they don't haunt you later. **First, every noun has a gender** — *o livro* (the book, masculine), *a mesa* (the table, feminine) — and that choice spreads to the articles and adjectives around it. **Second, verbs change form with the subject**, six forms for one verb; this is the price you pay for being able to drop the pronouns. **Third, there are two verbs for "to be"** — *ser* and *estar* — and picking the wrong one changes the meaning of your sentence, not just how it sounds.
That's why Unit 2 is all about gender and articles, Unit 3 is all about *ser* and *estar*, and verbs are taken apart from Unit 4 onward and never let go until the last unit.

One last thing makes this course different from most Portuguese materials out there: **what you learn here is the Portuguese of Portugal, not of Brazil.** They're one language and mutually intelligible, but they sound very different — the Portuguese swallow unstressed vowels until *telefone* sounds like "tluh-FOHN". The grammar differences are real too: in Portugal people say *chamo-me*, in Brazil *me chamo*; in Portugal *estou a comer*, in Brazil *estou comendo*. This course teaches the first, and flags the second whenever the difference matters.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Set aside 20-30 undisturbed minutes, not two hours broken into pieces. Languages stick through short, frequent repetition, not one long assault.

Read out loud — and in European Portuguese this isn't a suggestion, it's a requirement. The spelling shows letters whose sound has almost vanished; if you only read silently, your ear will never recognize the word when a Portuguese person says it.
Learn every noun **together with its article**: not *mesa*, but *a mesa*; not *livro*, but *o livro*. Ten extra seconds now saves months of confusion later.
Don't wait to be perfect before you dare to speak. The Portuguese are famously kind to foreigners who try their language — and far more used to hearing accents than you might expect.

blocks.text: Enjoy the journey. *Boa sorte!*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place.

blocks.text: This course is built for **self-study**. Each unit is designed to be finished in one sitting, about 20-30 minutes. What matters is not how fast you move forward, but how often you come back.
Every unit has the same layout, and the order is deliberate:

items: **Dialogue** — first read the Portuguese out loud without looking at the translation. Let your ears do the work before your brain demands an explanation.

**Literal translation** — the small italic line under the translation. This is the part people skip most often, yet it's where you see how Portuguese *thinks*. Example: *Como te chamas?* literally means "how yourself you-call?", not "what's your name".
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever just felt strange.
**Vocabulary** — the new words of the unit, each with its pronunciation.
**Exercises** — do them without looking at the key. Mistakes are part of the process.
**Answer key** — open it only after you've genuinely tried.

blocks.title: Spaced review
items: From Unit 3 on, each unit asks you to revisit an earlier unit — usually two steps back, just the right distance to make your memory work without feeling like starting over. Do it in reverse: cover the Portuguese, look at the English translation, and rebuild the Portuguese sentence from memory.
This is what turns "I understood it once" into "I can use it". Don't skip it.

blocks.title: Two habits of this course
items: **Nouns always come paired with their article.** In the vocabulary lists you'll always see *o carro*, *a casa* — never *carro* or *casa* on their own. Say them together, forever. A noun's gender can't be guessed from its meaning, and the only way to master it is never to separate it from its article from day one.

**The "Say it" column is written as heard, including the vowels that disappear.** If it gives *pequeno* as "puh-KAY-noo", that's not a typo — that's how people in Lisbon say it. Trust that column more than your eyes.

blocks.text: One last rule: **say it out loud**. European Portuguese is much harder to hear than to read. The only shortcut is to train your mouth first, so your ears have something to match.

This section is a bit long, and it's best not to memorize it in one go. Read it once now, then come back whenever the **Say it** column in a unit surprises you. After five or six units, you'll stop needing it.

Portuguese spelling is actually quite regular — far more honest than English. The difficulty isn't the letters but **what happens to unstressed vowels**. In Portugal they're weakened, shortened and often almost erased. That's what makes European Portuguese sound tight and hissing, while Brazilian Portuguese sounds open and lilting.

The **Say it** column throughout this course uses English-style spelling: *ah* as in *father*, *ay* as in *say*, *eh* as in *bed*, *ee* as in *see*, *oh* as in *go*, *aw* as in *law*, *oo* as in *food*, *uh* as in *about*, *ow* as in *now*, *y* as in *my* (on its own: *py* = "pie"). Capital letters mark the **stressed** syllable.

blocks.text: The **o** rule is the one that changes your accent fastest, and it has no exceptions: **every unstressed o is said oo.** *Portugal* → poor-too-GAHL. *Obrigado* → oo-bree-GAH-doo. *Como* → KOH-moo. If you take only one thing from this page, take this one.

blocks.text: This is where Portugal's typical hissing sound comes from. Every plural ends in *-s*, and every one of those *-s* is said **sh**: *os livros* → oosh LEE-vroosh. Brazilians say "os livros" with a plain s; the Portuguese, especially in Lisbon, hiss. If you want to sound like you learned in Portugal, this habit gives it away fastest.

blocks.text: The two most often mixed up: **nh** and **lh**. Both sounds already exist in English — the *ny* in "canyon" and the *lli* in "million" — so you don't need to learn a new sound, just trust that the two letters really merge into one.
Nasal vowels: the ~ mark and m/n at the end of a syllable

Portuguese has vowels that come out through the nose, like the vowel in French *bon*. This course writes them with an **n** after the vowel — *ahn*, *ohn*, *een*, *oon*, *own*, *ayn* — but don't pronounce a full n: let the vowel hum through your nose and stop before your tongue touches the roof of your mouth.

blocks.text: *Não* and *pão* are the first two words you'll say wrong, and that's normal. The key: it isn't "now", and it isn't "nown" with a real n — it's one whole sound coming out through the nose, starting from *a* and closing with rounded lips. Say "now" while pinching your nose shut; if you feel no buzz, you haven't nasalized it yet.

blocks.title: Three accents and what they mean
items: **´** (agudo) — the vowel is **open** and stressed: *café* (kuh-FEH), *avó* (uh-VAW) = grandmother.
**^** (circunflexo) — the vowel is **closed** and stressed: *português*, *avô* (uh-VOH) = grandfather. Look at *avó* and *avô*: one small mark separates grandma from grandpa.
**~** (til) — the vowel is **nasal**: *não*, *mãe*, *irmã*. The tilde doesn't always mark stress, but it almost always coincides with it.
**ç** (cedilha) — not an accent, but the way to write an **s** sound before a/o/u: *almoço*, *começar*. Without its tail, the *c* there would sound like *k*.

blocks.text: Finally, some comfort. You'll misread plenty of words in your first weeks, and it won't stop anyone from understanding you. Only two things really jar on Portuguese ears: **an o said as o** in an unstressed syllable, and **a final -s said as s**. Fix those two first; the rest will follow.
These pages aren't for studying — they're for a quick look when you forget a form in the middle of an exercise. Everything here has already been explained step by step in its own unit.
1. Articles and their contractions (Units 2, 7)
*de* + *um/uma* → *dum/duma*; *em* + *um/uma* → *num/numa*; *de* + *ele/ela* → *dele/dela*.
2. Ser, estar, ter, ir (Units 1, 3, 5, 8)
**ser** = permanent (identity, origin, profession, clock time). **estar** = temporary (feelings, location, states). **ter** = to have, age, hunger, have to. **ir** = to go, and "going to".
3. Present tense, regular verbs (Units 4, 5)
4. Past tense, regular verbs (Unit 14)
Portuguese spelling writes **falámos** with an accent for the past, and *falamos* without one for the present. Brazil writes both the same.
5. Possessives (Unit 5)
The article is **required** in Portugal: *o meu pai*, not *meu pai*. The form follows the thing owned, not the owner.
6. Demonstratives (Unit 16)
7. Pronouns (Units 11, 12)

**Position:** by default **after** the verb with a hyphen (*chamo-me*). It jumps **in front** after a negative (*não me chamo*), a question word (*como te chamas?*), a linking word (*que me diz*), or adverbs like *já*, *também*, *só*, *sempre*, *nunca*.
8. Irregular past tense (Unit 15)
9. The most common structures
These forty verbs cover most everyday conversation at A1. The last two columns give the *eu* form in the present and in the past — the two forms you'll need most often.

If you've reached this page and can tell the story of your weekend without stopping more than twice, you've completed level **A1** — the point where you can look after yourself in Portuguese: greet people, order, ask the way, shop, make plans, and talk about what's already happened.
Four things await you at the next level, and you've already had a peek at all of them in this course:

items: **The full imperfeito** — the second past tense you learned to recognize in Unit 20. At A2 you'll form it yourself, and your stories will instantly sound grown-up.

**The conjuntivo** (subjunctive) — the form for wishes, doubts and gentle requests: *espero que estejas bem*, *não me telefones antes das sete*. It has already appeared a few times in this course as a fixed block, without being taken apart.
**Combined pronouns** — *dá-mo* (*dá-me + o*), *diz-lho*. A typically Portuguese construction that trips up learners from everywhere.
**Vocabulary** — and this matters most. A1 grammar is almost enough for daily life; what limits you now is the number of words you know.

blocks.title: How to keep going on your own
items: **Listen to European Portuguese, not Brazilian.** RTP radio, the podcast *Falar Português*, and the news on RTP Play are all free. Your ear needs to get used to swallowed vowels — and Brazilian materials can't train that.
**Reread this course's dialogues out loud**, one unit a day, until you no longer need the translation. Twenty days, and the whole book moves into your mouth.
**Write five sentences every night** about your day. Not an essay — five sentences. It's the cheapest and most powerful exercise on this list.
**Find people to talk to.** The Portuguese are delighted when a foreigner makes the effort with the European variety; you'll be welcomed far more warmly than you expect.

blocks.text: And one last thing. You started this course knowing that *veranda* was once *varanda* and *marmalade* was *marmelada*. Now you know that the language behind them isn't just a source of a few borrowed words — it's a whole way of building sentences that, after twenty units, is starting to become your own.
*Boa sorte, e até breve!*
